extraction_text: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about how members of the Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra castes can attain Brahmin status.
Bhishma explains that Brahmin status is the highest and not easily attained by other castes, citing an ancient story about Matanga and a female donkey.
Matanga's father sends him to gather materials for a sacrifice, and Matanga drives a cart pulled by a young donkey.
The young donkey keeps veering toward its mother, so Matanga beats it with a stick.
The female donkey sees her injured child and tells it that the driver is a Chandala, not a Brahmin, because Brahmins are compassionate and would not abuse animals.

attributes.relationship: Mother comforts child, reveals truth about Matanga

extraction_text: Matanga hears the donkey's words, jumps from the cart, and demands to know why he is a Chandala and lost Brahmin status.
The female donkey reveals that Matanga was born from a Brahmin woman and a Shudra barber, making him a Chandala by birth.
Matanga returns home, and his father questions why he abandoned the task.
Matanga begins to respond, but the text cuts off mid-sentence.

attributes.note: Text ends abruptly with Matanga starting to speak

extraction_text: Matanga questions his father about his mother's identity and expresses discomfort with his mixed parentage.

attributes.relationships: Matanga learns from his mother (a donkey) that he is born of a Brahmin woman and a Shudra father, causing him distress about his social status.

extraction_text: Matanga decides to leave home to perform severe austerities (tapas) to attain Brahmin status.

attributes.relationships: Matanga abandons his family life to pursue spiritual goals.

extraction_text: Matanga performs intense austerities in a great forest, generating immense heat that affects the gods.

attributes.supernatural_elements: His tapas generates heat that troubles the gods (devas).

extraction_text: Indra (the wielder of brown horses, the destroyer of cities) appears before Matanga and offers him a boon.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Indra, king of gods, manifests due to the power of Matanga's austerities.

extraction_text: Matanga asks Indra for the status of a Brahmin as his boon.

attributes.relationships: Matanga seeks to change his inherent social status through divine means.

extraction_text: Indra refuses, stating that an impure soul cannot attain Brahmin status and that such a high goal is unattainable for one born as a Chandala.

attributes.relationships: Indra asserts the fixed nature of varna (social order) and warns Matanga of the dangers of his ambition.

extraction_text: Matanga remains steadfast in his vow and performs even more severe austerity, standing on one leg for a hundred years.
Indra appears again, reiterating that the highest status is extremely difficult to attain and advising Matanga to abandon his pursuit as it is not the righteous path.

attributes.relationships: Indra continues to dissuade Matanga, emphasizing the impossibility and peril of his goal.

extraction_text: Indra explains the gradual process of rebirth through lower forms (animals, outcastes, Shudras, Vaishyas) before potentially reaching Kshatriya status over immense periods.

attributes.relationships: Indra outlines the cosmic law of gradual spiritual and social evolution through countless rebirths, contrasting with Matanga's desire for immediate transformation.

extraction_text: Indra explained to Matanga the extreme difficulty of achieving Brahmin status through multiple rebirths over immense time periods.
Hearing Indra's words, Matanga fell into deep sorrow and went to the Gaya River to perform severe penance, standing on one big toe for one hundred years.
Matanga's body became extremely weak from the penance - emaciated, with exposed veins, reduced to skin and bones - until he collapsed from exhaustion.
Vasava (Indra) quickly arrived and caught the falling Matanga, showing his role as benefactor and protector of beings.
Indra explained the importance and rarity of Brahmin status, emphasizing that Brahmins protect all beings' welfare and please gods and ancestors.
Matanga responded with despair, questioning why Indra would make him suffer more when he's already tormented, and criticizing those who don't value the hard-won Brahmin status.
A Brahmin who does not protect his status is compared to someone who wins rare wealth but does not guard it, considered the greatest sinner among sinners.
The Brahmin status is described as difficult to obtain and even harder to maintain, criticizing those who obtain it but do not protect it.
A speaker questions why someone like them, who is self-content, free from opposites, non-violent, self-controlled, and charitable, cannot be a Brahmin, while others who neglect it can.
The speaker requests the ability to choose any pleasure, change form, fly, be respected by Brahmins and Kshatriyas, and have immortal fame.
Indra grants the boon, stating the speaker will be widely known as the god of sacred hymns and become an object of worship for women.
After granting the boon to Matanga, Indra disappears, and Matanga stops breathing, attaining the highest status.
Bhishma concludes that Indra spoke correctly, affirming that the supreme status called Brahmin is difficult to obtain.
